did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a heading attributing it to Moses and presents the Lord as humanity’s dwelling place—a home and refuge—in every generation.
Did you know? Before describing the creation of the mountains and the earth, the psalm presents the Lord as existing “from everlasting to everlasting,” beyond human and worldly time.

Did you know? The psalm compares a thousand years in the Lord’s sight to yesterday and to “a watch in the night”—a brief period during the night—to emphasize the difference between divine and human time.
Did you know? Human life is described as being quickly swept away and like passing sleep, and then as grass that grows and withers.
Did you know? The image of grass emphasizes the brevity of life through the cycle of morning and evening: it sprouts in the morning, fades, and by evening withers and dries up.
Did you know? In the psalm, the brevity of life is also connected to the human experience of being under the Lord’s anger and wrath: “For we are consumed by Your anger.”
Did you know? The psalm emphasizes that nothing is hidden from the Lord: human sins and secret faults lie exposed before Him, revealed by the light of His presence.
Did you know? The psalm gives a normal life span as seventy years, or eighty if one is strong, but adds that even these years are filled with toil and trouble and pass quickly.
Did you know? At the heart of the prayer is a request to turn awareness of life’s brevity into wisdom: “Teach us to number our days” so that we may gain a heart of wisdom.
Did you know? The psalm’s conclusion asks not only for divine favor, but also for the Lord to establish and sustain the work of human hands—a request repeated twice in the same verse.
